body:
Seamless web communication feels effortless today. But building a low-latency video or voice streaming app used to be a major hurdle for developers. Users had to deal with dropped frames, audio lag, and disconnections that marred interactions.

WebRTC helps developers address shortcomings in real-time web communications by enabling low-latency peer-to-peer data streaming. Since its introduction in 2011, major browsers, including Chrome, Safari, and Firefox, have adopted WebRTC. Today, WebRTC supports real-time communication in browsers and web apps.

This article explores how WebRTC works, its use cases, security considerations, and how it compares with other web communication technologies.

## Summary

• WebRTC is a technology that allows peer-to-peer real-time streaming of audio, video, and data between browsers or web apps.

• WebRTC operates with UDP, making it suitable for low-latency, loss-tolerant web communication applications.

• To stream with WebRTC, you use standard APIs such as RTCPeerConnection, MediaStream, and RTCDataChannel, which create an encrypted channel for real-time media exchange.

• Peer devices rely on STUN and TURN servers to discover their IP address and overcome network restrictions when establishing WebRTC connections.

• Developers must consider several challenges, including scalability, security, and connectivity, when building WebRTC applications.

## What is WebRTC?

WebRTC is a free, open-source communication technology that enables peer-to-peer, real-time streaming between web browsers. With WebRTC, users can exchange video, audio, and data directly without downloading plugins or intermediary software.

Unlike traditional client-server streaming, WebRTC sends media directly between peers whenever a direct path exists. Relay (TURN) servers and media servers step in only when a direct connection isn’t possible or when more than two participants join. This allows WebRTC to deliver low-latency real-time media.

Modern web browsers support WebRTC by default. WebRTC is an open standard from the W3C and IETF that exposes JavaScript APIs, which let you access the camera and microphone, create a data channel, and deliver media content to the destination.

Because of its simplicity, developers use WebRTC to power various web applications, including teleconferencing, video and audio streaming, real-time transcription, and screen sharing.

## How WebRTC works: from signaling to peer-to-peer media

WebRTC captures data in a browser, encrypts it, and streams it to another browser in real time. It creates a data channel over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), where browsers or web apps can exchange data with low latency. UDP is a fast, connectionless protocol that sends data packets across networks. It doesn’t need to maintain a connection, acknowledge packet reception, or retransmit lost packets, resulting in significantly lower overhead.

By default, the native WebRTC API supports direct peer-to-peer (P2P) streaming between two browsers. However, more than two browsers can exchange data by creating multiple P2P connections or using a media server. Often, upstream bandwidth limits multiple P2P connections, making a media server a better option for applications like live conferencing.

Below, we use an example that demonstrates video between two browsers to explain how it works.

To create a WebRTC connection, both browsers follow these sequences.

• Media capture. Before capturing data, the browser asks the user for permission to access their microphone, camera, or screen. This is a default security feature built within the WebRTC framework that developers cannot bypass.

• Signaling. This process lets both browsers negotiate metadata through signaling servers to enable successful data exchange. For example, browser A sends the codec, bitrate, and encryption technologies it supports. Then, it waits for browser B to respond with corresponding metadata. Both browsers must agree on a common set of metadata before they can exchange data.

• Securing the channel. WebRTC encrypts media and data in transit to protect them from unauthorized parties. Both browsers exchange cryptographic keys using the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS), which they use to encrypt and decrypt data. Each hop is encrypted separately, so a media server or SFU can access the media unless you add end-to-end encryption on top, for example with insertable streams.

• Media exchange. Once the browsers have negotiated a cryptographic key, they exchange media using the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP). The sender will encrypt all outgoing video, audio, and other arbitrary data using AES-128. Meanwhile, the device uses the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) to send arbitrary data such as JSON and text files.

• Congestion management. Devices actively detect jitter, lags, or other signs of degradation. A device sends Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP) packets to a peer. Then, it examines the RTCP response using a bandwidth estimation algorithm called Google Congestion Control and adjusts its transmission rate accordingly.

The WebRTC standards provide application programming interfaces (API) and guidelines for media capture, data security, and media exchange. However, it doesn’t define a signaling framework. Therefore, developers implement signaling through different mechanisms, such as WebSockets.

## Supported WebRTC codecs

A codec is an algorithm that compresses and decompresses media streams. All WebRTC-compliant browsers must support the following codecs.

• Audio: Opus, G.711 PCM (A-law), G.711 PCM (µ-law).

However, some browsers may support newer codecs, such as AV1 and VP9.
